Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. That $R_{abcd}$ are the components of a smooth $(0,4)$-tensor
field and that $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$ are the components of a smooth
symmetric $(0,2)$-tensor field, so that the contractions above are
basis-independent and do not depend on the chart, is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clauses (a)-(d); the Ricci symmetry
is part of that statement.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector
$n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$. Because
$g_p(n,n)=-1\neq0$, an observer is timelike and in particular nonzero
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Observers at $p$ exist:
the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and
$n:=N_p/\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}$ satisfies $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and
$g_p(n,N_p)=-\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}<0$, where the square root is the
nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]; then $-n$ is a unit timelike
vector with $g_p(-n,N_p)>0$, so it is not an observer, and the two vectors
$n,-n$ point in opposite time directions.

**(b) Rest space.** For an observer $n$ at $p$, the **rest space** of $n$ is
the $g_p$-orthogonal complement of the line $\mathbb Rn$,

$$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM: g_p(v,n)=0\},$$

in the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. It is
a linear subspace of $T_pM$. The further facts that $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and
that the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite are proved
in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]; they are consequences, not
part of the definition.

**(c) Spatial projection.** The **spatial projection** of the observer $n$ is
the map

$$h_n:T_pM\longrightarrow T_pM,\qquad h_n(v):=v+g_p(n,v)\,n .$$

The map is linear because $g_p$ is bilinear, its image is contained in
$n^{\perp}$, and it fixes $n^{\perp}$ pointwise; that it is the
$g_p$-orthogonal projection onto $n^{\perp}$ with kernel $\mathbb Rn$ is
proved in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]].

**(d) Scope.** An observer at $p$ is a single tangent vector. It is not an
ordered basis or frame of $T_pM$, not a chart, not a field of observers such as
the congruences defined later on this page, and not a curve or a worldline: no
parametrized curve, clock reading, proper time or measurement is attached to
$n$ by this definition. The physical reading of an observer as the direction
of an ideal clock's worldline, and the measurement interpretation of the
observer-relative quantities introduced later on this page, belong to the
physical postulates and unit conventions of the framework and are not asserted
here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, $p\in M$,
$n$ an observer at $p$ and $P\in T_pM$ a future timelike vector with rest
mass $m:=m(P)>0$ ([[def-gr-observer-relative-energy-and-momentum]],
[[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]). Write $U:=P/m$, $u:=U/c$,
$\gamma:=-g_p(n,u)$ and, as in clause 3 of
[[lem-gr-observer-energy-momentum-identities]],

$$w:=\frac{c\,h_n(u)}{\gamma}\in n^\perp,\qquad s:=\sqrt{g_p(w,w)} .$$

For $z\in n^\perp$ write $|z|_n:=\sqrt{g_p(z,z)}$, the norm from the positive-definite restriction of $g_p$ to $n^\perp$. Thus $s=|w|_n$, and $|q_n(P)|$ in the displays below means $|q_n(P)|_n$; $q_n(P)\in n^\perp$ by the observer decomposition.

Then $s<c$, $\gamma=(1-s^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$,

$$E_n(P)=mc^2\Bigl(1-\frac{s^2}{c^2}\Bigr)^{-1/2},\qquad |q_n(P)|=ms\Bigl(1-\frac{s^2}{c^2}\Bigr)^{-1/2},$$

and for every $0\le v_0<c$, with $z_0:=v_0^2/c^2<1$ and all $s\le v_0$,

$$\Bigl|E_n(P)-mc^2-\tfrac12ms^2\Bigr|\le\tfrac38\,(1-z_0)^{-5/2}\,\frac{ms^4}{c^2},\qquad \Bigl||q_n(P)|-ms\Bigr|\le\tfrac12\,(1-z_0)^{-3/2}\,\frac{ms^3}{c^2} .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and let
$U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open subset, the **matter domain**, carrying its
restricted smooth structure
([[prop-an-open-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold-has-a-canonical-restricted-smooth-structure]]).

**(a) Data.** A **dust model** on $U$ is a pair $(\rho,u)$ consisting of

- a smooth function $\rho:U\to\mathbb R$ with $\rho(p)>0$ for every $p\in U$,
  the **rest density**; and
- a smooth future-directed unit timelike vector field $u$ on $U$
  ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]] with target $TM$
  described through the tangent bundle; concretely, $u$ is a smooth vector
  field on $U$ with $g_p(u_p,u_p)=-1$ and $g_p(u_p,N_p)<0$ at every $p$,
  [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

The parameter $\rho$ is the coefficient in the unit-normalized tensor of
clause (b); this mathematical definition assigns it no physical unit. In the
framework's SI stress-energy reading it is the **rest energy density**
$\varepsilon:=\rho$, in $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}$. The **rest-mass
density** is instead $\rho_m:=\varepsilon/c^2$, in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-3}$, and the physical four-velocity is
$U:=cu$, with $g(U,U)=-c^2$. Thus the same tensor is
$T^{ab}=\varepsilon u^au^b=\rho_m U^aU^b$. A purely mathematical or
$c=1$ convention may rescale the density coefficient; interpreting $\rho$
as an SI mass density while keeping the unit tangent $u$ would require the
explicit tensor $c^2\rho\,u\otimes u$. Physical realizations and readings
are adopted by the matter postulate, not deduced here.

**(b) Stress-energy tensor.** The model's **stress-energy tensor** is the
smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field

$$T^{ab}:=\rho\,u^au^b\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad T_{ab}=\rho\,u_au_b,$$

with $u_a=g_{ac}u^c$ ([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]); the two expressions correspond
under raising both indices, by $g^{ac}g^{bd}T_{cd}=T^{ab}$.

**(c) Dust system.** The **dust system** on $U$ is the pair of equations

$$\nabla_a(\rho\,u^a)=0,\qquad u^a\nabla_au^b=0 .$$

The first is a continuity equation for the density current $\rho u$; the
second says that the integral curves of $u$ are geodesics in the parameter that
makes $u$ their unit tangent, i.e. that the dust particles are in free fall
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]).

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$ and let $U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open
matter domain ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[prop-an-open-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold-has-a-canonical-restricted-smooth-structure]]).

**(a) Dust.** Let $(\rho,u,T)$ be a dust model on $U$
([[def-gr-dust-matter-model]]). Then

$$\nabla^aT_{ab}=0\ \text{on }U\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \nabla_a(\rho u^a)=0\ \text{and}\ u^a\nabla_au^b=0\ \text{on }U .$$

**(b) Perfect fluid.** Let $(\varepsilon,p,n,T)$ be a perfect-fluid model on
$U$ with comoving derivative $D$, expansion $\vartheta$, acceleration $a$ and
projection $h$ ([[def-gr-perfect-fluid-matter-model]]). Then

$$\nabla^aT_{ab}=0\ \text{on }U\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+p)\vartheta=0\quad\text{and}\quad (\varepsilon+p)a^b+h^{ba}\partial_ap=0\ \text{on }U .$$
For $n\ge1$, $c\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and $r>0$, the Euclidean closed ball $\overline B_2(c,r)$ and Euclidean sphere $S_2(c,r)$ are compact.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-taylor-schlomilch-roche-remainder]], there are points $\xi_L,\xi_C$ between $a$ and $x$ such that
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_L)}{\iota((n+1)!)}(x-a)^{n+1}$$
and
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_C)}{\iota(n!)}(x-\xi_C)^n(x-a).$$

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

derivations.claim: (A compact two-jet estimate independent of the spatial compact.) Identify the finite-dimensional vector space of symmetric metric two-jets $(A,L\partial A,L^2\partial^2A)$ with $\mathbb R^N$ and give it its Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$. In the length-coordinate chart the Christoffel and curvature formulas make $L^2G_{ab}(\eta+A)$ a rational smooth function $F_{ab}(J)$ of the two-jet $J$, wherever $\eta+A$ is invertible; its denominators are powers of $\det(\eta+A)$. Choose $0<\delta<1/16$ and let $Q=\overline B_2(0,\delta)\subset\mathbb R^N$. For $J\in Q$, every entry of $A$ has absolute value at most $\delta$. Put $H=\eta^{-1}A$; since $\eta^{-1}$ is diagonal with entries $\pm1$, $m(H)\le\delta$. Each entry of a product of $4\times4$ matrices is a sum of four products, so the finite-product estimate $m(BD)\le4m(B)m(D)$, $m(H^k)\le4^{k-1}\delta^k\le(4\delta)^k$ for $k\ge1$, so the matrix series $\sum_{k\ge0}(-H)^k$ converges entrywise by [L8]. The finite identity $(I+H)\sum_{k=0}^N(-H)^k=\sum_{k=0}^N(-H)^k(I+H)=I+(-1)^NH^{N+1}$ and $m(H^{N+1})\to0$ show that its sum is $(I+H)^{-1}$. The same argument applies on a neighborhood of $Q$, so $F_{ab}$ is smooth there. By [L8], $Q$ is compact and $D^2F_{ab}$ has a bound $M$ on $Q$ depending only on $\delta$ and the dimension, not on $K$ or on the family. Also $F_{ab}(0)=0$ and $DF_{ab}(0)[J]=L^2G^{(1)}_{ab}$ by [L3]. Applying the Lagrange remainder of [L8] to $t\mapsto F_{ab}(tJ)$ gives $|G_{ab}(\eta+A)-G^{(1)}_{ab}(A)|\le (M/2)\|J\|_2^2/L^2$ whenever $J\in Q$. By [L1], for $\varepsilon\le1$ the jet vector $J_L(A(\varepsilon),p)$ has norm at most $C_0(C)\varepsilon$ on $\pi^{-1}(K)\cap\Omega$, since all time derivatives vanish. Choose $\varepsilon_*'$ small enough that this norm is at most $\delta$. This proves (a) with a constant independent of $K$.

(The diagonal first-order term.) Define the stationary symmetric tensor $h$ on $U$ by $h_{00}=-2\varphi$, $h_{ij}=-2\varphi\delta_{ij}$ and $h_{0i}=0$. Then $A(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon h+s(\varepsilon)$, where $s_{00}=r_{00}$, $s_{0i}=r_{0i}$ and $s_{ij}=r_{ij}$. For $h$, its trace is $-4\varphi$, so $\bar h_{00}=-4\varphi$ and all $\bar h_{0i},\bar h_{ij}$ vanish. Formula [L3] and stationarity give $G^{(1)}_{00}(h)=2\Delta\varphi$, $G^{(1)}_{0i}(h)=0$ and $G^{(1)}_{ij}(h)=0$.

(Dust conservation and the coordinate energy component.) First, normalization and the Einstein equation give $\mathcal E_\varepsilon=-g^{ab}T_{ab}=-\kappa^{-1}g^{ab}G_{ab}$; the spatial factorization of the metric, inverse and curvature makes this a spatial function, even across disconnected time fibers. The dust equations in [A1] give, by the product rule and metric compatibility, $
abla^{\varepsilon a}T_{ab}=u_b
abla^\varepsilon_a(\mathcal E u^a)+\mathcal E u^a
abla^\varepsilon_a u_b=0$ on all of $\Omega$, including points where $\mathcal E=0$; no division by density is used. This is the forward conservation implication of [L7], extended to the nonnegative branch. By [L2], $g_{00}\le-1/2$ on $K$, so put $\alpha=\sqrt{-g_{00}}>0$, so $\partial_0=\alpha n$ and $n=n_\varepsilon$ is a future unit observer by the time-orientation condition in the Statement. By [L6], $\gamma^2=(1-s^2/c^2)^{-1}$. Since $s^2/c^2\le C^2\varepsilon\le1/4$, $\gamma^2\le4/3$ and $\gamma^2-1\le(4/3)C^2\varepsilon$. The weak-field coefficient gives $|\alpha^2-1|=|-g_{00}-1|\le2C\varepsilon+C\varepsilon^2\le3C\varepsilon$. Also $(u_\varepsilon)_0=g(u_\varepsilon,\partial_0)=-\alpha\gamma$, whence $T_{00}=\mathcal E_\varepsilon\alpha^2\gamma^2$. It follows that $|\alpha^2\gamma^2-1|\le\gamma^2|\alpha^2-1|+(\gamma^2-1)\le(4C+	frac43C^2)\varepsilon$. The energy bound of [A1] now gives $|T_{00}-\mu_\varepsilon c^2|\le C_d\varepsilon^2c^4/(G_NL^2)$ with $C_d:=4C^2+	frac43C^3$, and division by $c^2$ gives the stated estimate for $|ho_\varepsilon-\mu_\varepsilon|$.

(Linear splitting.) The operator $G^{(1)}$ of [L3] is linear in its tensor argument. Thus $G^{(1)}(A(\varepsilon))=\varepsilon G^{(1)}(h)+G^{(1)}(s(\varepsilon))$. Combining this with step 1.1 yields $G(g(\varepsilon))=\varepsilon G^{(1)}(h)+G^{(1)}(s(\varepsilon))+O(C_0^2\varepsilon^2/L^2)$ with a uniform componentwise constant.

(Remainder-component bounds.) The terms in $G^{(1)}(s)$ involve only second derivatives of $s$. By [L1], $|G^{(1)}_{ij}(s)|\le C'\varepsilon^2/L^2$ and $|G^{(1)}_{0i}(s)|\le C'\varepsilon^{3/2}/L^2$. In the $00$ component, $s_{0i}$ contributes only through terms with a time derivative or a contraction by $\eta^{0i}$, both zero by [L4] and $\eta^{0i}=0$; hence $|G^{(1)}_{00}(s)|\le C'\varepsilon^2/L^2$.

(Einstein-tensor hierarchy.) Steps 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1 show $G_{00}=2\varepsilon\Delta\varphi+O(\varepsilon^2/L^2)=2\Delta\Phi/c^2+O(\varepsilon^2/L^2)$, $G_{ij}=O(\varepsilon^2/L^2)$ and $G_{0i}=O(\varepsilon^{3/2}/L^2)$. Taking a sufficiently large constant $C_2^0(C,L)$ proves (b). By the Einstein-family condition and $\rho_\varepsilon=T_{00}/c^2$, the first stress estimate also gives $|\Delta\Phi-4\pi G_N\rho_\varepsilon|\le C_2^0\varepsilon^2c^2/(2L^2)$ for all such families.

(Poisson matching to the independent dust density.) From [L5] and step 4.1, $|\kappa T_{00}-2\Delta\Phi/c^2|\le C_2^0\varepsilon^2/L^2$. Write $T_{00}=\mu_\varepsilon c^2+\eta_\varepsilon$, where step 1.3 gives $|\eta_\varepsilon|\le C_d\varepsilon^2c^4/(G_NL^2)$. Since $\kappa=8\pi G_N/c^4$, multiplication by $c^2/2$ yields $|\Delta\Phi-4\pi G_N\mu_\varepsilon|\le(C_2^0/2+4\pi C_d)\varepsilon^2c^2/L^2$. Enlarge $C_2\ge C_2^0$ to cover this constant and all component bounds. The comparison is with the independent rest-mass density, not with the definitionally read $T_{00}/c^2$.

(Scaled source and conclusion.) For $X\in K/L$, $\Delta_X\psi(X)=L^2\Delta\varphi(LX)$ and $4\pi R(X)=4\pi G_NL^2\mu_\varepsilon(LX)/(\varepsilon c^2)$. Multiplying the estimate of step 5.1 at $LX$ by $L^2/(\varepsilon c^2)$ gives $|\Delta_X\psi-4\pi R|\le C_2\varepsilon$. This proves (d), and steps 1.1, 4.1 and 1.3-5.1 prove (a)-(c).

step 1.2 computes the exact first-order coefficient G^(1) of the diagonal perturbation h and step 4.1 shows the leading term of G_{00} is 2εΔφ; the zero case of the linearized perturbation s(ε) is the case treated exactly in step 1.2.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 invokes the quadratic remainder input [L2] with the smallness threshold, so the metric family stays within the Lorentzian regime where the expansion is valid; the degenerate branch is excluded by the explicit ε_*'.

boundaries.reason: The bounds are on K for 0 < ε ≤ ε_*'; the threshold ε_*' is interior to the admissible range and no endpoint value is evaluated.
ε_*' and C₂ are produced by explicit compactness and Taylor arguments from C, L and the dimension; no selection occurs.
The theorem states component inequalities and a conditional Poisson estimate, not an equivalence.
No converse (for example that every prescribed density admits such data) is asserted; the existence of the family is a hypothesis.

citations.quote:
Let $(\Omega,K,L,C,\varepsilon_0,\varphi,r)$ be stationary weak-field data
with spatial base $U=\pi(\Omega)$, compact $K\subseteq U$, and spatial
potential $\Phi=\varepsilon c^2\varphi:U\to\mathbb R$
([[def-gr-stationary-weak-field-data]]), let $c>0$, and let
$\varepsilon_*$ and $C_1$ be the threshold and constant of
[[lem-gr-weak-field-admissibility-and-inverse-bounds]]. Then there is
$C_2<\infty$, depending only on $C$, $L$ and the dimension, such that for
every $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_*$ the Christoffel symbols
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of the metric-selected connection of $g(\varepsilon)$ in
the inertial chart satisfy the following bounds at every spacetime point
$p\in\Omega$ with $\pi(p)\in K$:

$$\Bigl|\Gamma^i{}_{00}-\frac{\partial_i\Phi}{c^2}\Bigr|\le\frac{C_2\varepsilon^2}{L},\qquad |\Gamma^i{}_{0j}|\le\frac{C_2\varepsilon^{3/2}}{L},\qquad |\Gamma^i{}_{jk}|\le\frac{C_2\varepsilon}{L},$$

$$|\Gamma^0{}_{00}|\le\frac{C_2\varepsilon^{5/2}}{L},\qquad |\Gamma^0{}_{0j}|\le\frac{C_2\varepsilon}{L},\qquad |\Gamma^0{}_{jk}|\le\frac{C_2\varepsilon^{3/2}}{L},$$

for all $i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$, with the maximum over the free spatial indices.

Let $(M,g_\eta,N_\eta)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]] with inertial chart
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ and constant components
$\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. Let $\Omega\subseteq M$ be a
nonempty open spacetime region, identified with its image in $\mathbb R^4$,
and let $\pi:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ be the spatial projection
$\pi(x^0,\mathbf x)=\mathbf x$. Its image $U:=\pi(\Omega)$ is open: a
coordinate ball in $\Omega$ about any point projects onto a ball about that
point's spatial coordinates. Let $K\subseteq U$ be compact. Let $c>0$ and
$G_N>0$ be the constants of the framework's conventions and put
$\kappa:=8\pi G_N/c^4$. The coordinates have units of metres, $c$ has units
$\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$, and $\varepsilon$ is dimensionless.

**(a) Structural data.** A tuple $(\Omega,K,L,C,\varepsilon_0,\varphi,r)$ is
**stationary weak-field data** when

- $L>0$ is a length, $C>0$ is dimensionless, and $\varepsilon_0>0$ is
  dimensionless;
- $\varphi:U\to\mathbb R$ is a smooth dimensionless spatial function and
  $r=(r_{ab})$ is a family of smooth dimensionless spatial functions
  $r_{ab}:(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)\times U\to\mathbb R$ for some
  $\varepsilon_1>\varepsilon_0$
  ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]);
- for every $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$ the component field

$$g_{ab}(\varepsilon,p)=\begin{cases}-(1+2\varepsilon\varphi(\pi(p)))+r_{00}(\varepsilon,\pi(p)),&a=b=0,\\[2pt] r_{0i}(\varepsilon,\pi(p)),&\{a,b\}=\{0,i\},\\[2pt] (1-2\varepsilon\varphi(\pi(p)))\,\delta_{ij}+r_{ij}(\varepsilon,\pi(p)),&a=i,\ b=j,\end{cases}$$

  is the component field of a smooth Lorentzian metric $g(\varepsilon)$ on
  $\Omega$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]);
- **(spatial factorization and stationarity)** all metric components factor
  through $\pi$ by construction. Thus points of $\Omega$ with the same
  spatial coordinates have the same metric components, even when they lie in
  different connected components of that spatial fiber, and
  $\partial_0g_{ab}=0$ on $\Omega$;
- **(spatial bounds)** for every multiindex $\alpha\in\mathbb N^3$ with
  $|\alpha|\le2$ and every $\mathbf x\in K$,

$$|\partial^\alpha\varphi(\mathbf x)|\le\frac{C}{L^{|\alpha|}},\qquad |\partial^\alpha r_{00}(\varepsilon,\mathbf x)|+|\partial^\alpha r_{ij}(\varepsilon,\mathbf x)|\le\frac{C\varepsilon^2}{L^{|\alpha|}},\qquad |\partial^\alpha r_{0i}(\varepsilon,\mathbf x)|\le\frac{C\varepsilon^{3/2}}{L^{|\alpha|}}.$$

  (Derivatives are with respect to $x^1,x^2,x^3$; here $|\partial^\alpha r_{ij}|$
  is the maximum over $i,j$ and $|\partial^\alpha r_{0i}|$ is the maximum
  over $i$.)

**(b) Derived data.** For stationary weak-field data define the
**spatial potential**

$$\Phi:=\varepsilon c^2\varphi\qquad\text{on }U,$$

a smooth spatial function of dimension $\mathrm m^2\,\mathrm s^{-2}$ in the
framework's unit conventions; its pullback to $\Omega$ is stationary. The
symmetric component family $g(\varepsilon)-\eta$ is the **perturbation of the
family**.

**(c) Einstein families.** Stationary weak-field data form an **Einstein
family with coupling $\kappa$** when for every $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$
there is a smooth symmetric component field $T_{ab}(\varepsilon,\cdot)$ on
$\Omega$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) satisfying

$$G_{ab}\bigl(g(\varepsilon)\bigr)=\kappa\,T_{ab}(\varepsilon)\qquad\text{on }\Omega,$$

where $G$ is the Einstein tensor of the metric-selected connection of
$g(\varepsilon)$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). In that case define the
**spatial density read from the time-time component**

$$\rho_\varepsilon(\mathbf x):=\frac{T_{00}(\varepsilon,x^0,\mathbf x)}{c^2}\qquad\text{on }U,$$

where any $x^0$ with $(x^0,\mathbf x)\in\Omega$ may be used. This is
well-defined: the metric is the pullback of spatial functions, so its
coordinate curvature components, and hence $T_{00}=\kappa^{-1}G_{00}$, are
constant on each fiber of $\pi$, including when that fiber is disconnected.
It has units $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-3}$; it is a coordinate-component
density and is not thereby the dust rest-mass density.

**(d) Scope.** This item fixes a class of metric families and the vocabulary
of the weak-field bridge: the spatial factorization, component form,
stationarity, spatial derivative bounds, potential, and the equation that
upgrades the data to an Einstein family. It asserts neither existence for prescribed data nor that $\partial_0$ is
timelike or a Killing field, that the inverse metrics are uniformly bounded,
or that $\rho_\varepsilon$ is positive; the latter properties are
consequences proved separately where they are used. The family is an explicit
input-family hypothesis: neither its existence for prescribed Newtonian
initial data nor its construction from other data is claimed. The physical
reading of the components, of $G_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}$, of $\Phi$ and of
$\rho_\varepsilon$ belongs to the framework's postulates and unit
conventions, which are separate items.

Let $(\Omega,K,L,C,\varepsilon_0,\varphi,r)$ be stationary weak-field data
with spatial base $U=\pi(\Omega)$ and compact $K\subseteq U$
([[def-gr-stationary-weak-field-data]], [[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]]),
and let $E(\varepsilon):=g(\varepsilon)-\eta$ and
$H(\varepsilon):=\eta^{-1}E(\varepsilon)$ be the component matrices of the
perturbation and of its $\eta$-raise. Let
$m(A):=\max_{a,b}|A_{ab}|$ denote the maximum-entry norm of a $4\times4$
matrix. Then with
$\varepsilon_*:=\min\{\varepsilon_0,\,1,\,(128C)^{-1}\}$ the following
hold at every $p\in\Omega$ with $\pi(p)\in K$ and every
$0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_*$:

**(a) Smallness, timelikeness and stationarity.** At these spacetime points,

$$m\bigl(E(\varepsilon)\bigr)\le4C\varepsilon,\qquad m\bigl(H(\varepsilon)\bigr)\le16C\varepsilon\le\tfrac18,\qquad g(\varepsilon)_{00}\le-\tfrac12 ,$$

so the chart field $\partial_0$ is timelike over the spatial compact $K$;
moreover $\partial_0$ is
a Killing field of $g(\varepsilon)$ on $\Omega$
([[def-gr-killing-field]]).

**(b) Inverse-metric expansion and uniform bounds.** There is
$C_1=C_1(C,L)<\infty$ such that at these spacetime points, with
$R^{ab}(\varepsilon):=g^{ab}(\varepsilon)-\eta^{ab}+\eta^{ac}E_{cd}(\varepsilon)\eta^{db}$,

$$|R^{ab}(\varepsilon)|\le C_1\varepsilon^2,\qquad |g^{ab}(\varepsilon)-\eta^{ab}|\le C_1\varepsilon,\qquad |\partial^\alpha g^{ab}(\varepsilon)|\le\frac{C_1}{L^{|\alpha|}}\quad(1\le|\alpha|\le2),$$

and

$$|\partial^\alpha R^{ab}(\varepsilon)|\le\frac{C_1\varepsilon^2}{L^{|\alpha|}}\qquad(0\le|\alpha|\le2),$$

where $g^{ab}(\varepsilon)$ are the components of the inverse metric
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]).

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\nabla$ be an affine connection
on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]). Smooth vector fields
are smooth sections of the tangent bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]); as there, their use
rests on the canonical smooth structure of $TM$, which assumes the axiom
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]]. This is the only use of that
axiom in this definition.

**(a) Metric compatibility.** The connection $\nabla$ is **$g$-compatible**, or
**compatible with the metric** $g$, when for all smooth vector fields $X,Y,Z$ on
$M$ the identity of smooth functions

$$X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$$

holds on $M$. Here $g(Y,Z)$ is the smooth function $p\mapsto g_p(Y_p,Z_p)$ and
$X$ acts on functions as a derivation; the identity uses only the action of
$\nabla$ on vector fields and requires no extension of $\nabla$ to tensor
fields. When such an extension is available, this identity is the statement
$\nabla_Xg=0$, and the compatibility of $\nabla$ with the inverse metric
$g^{-1}$ follows; neither statement is part of this definition.

**(b) Torsion freedom.** The **torsion** of $\nabla$ is the tangent-valued
$2$-tensor $T(X,Y)=\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX-[X,Y]$ of
[[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]], with bracket as in
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. The connection is **torsion-free**
when $T(X,Y)=0$ for all smooth $X,Y$, that is, when
$\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$ identically.

**(c) Metric-selected connections.** A **metric-selected connection** for
$(M,g)$ is an affine connection on $M$ that is both torsion-free and
$g$-compatible. Equivalently, it is an element of the class

$$\operatorname{LC}(M,g):=\{\nabla:\nabla\text{ is an affine connection on }M,\ \nabla\text{ is torsion-free and }g\text{-compatible}\}.$$

The name records that the pair of conditions selects the connection out of all
affine connections; it is the pair of conditions imposed on the connection that
conventional general relativity uses, and the connection so selected is called
the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.


**(d) Intrinsic construction before physical use.** For smooth local vector
fields define the Koszul expression

$$K(X,Y,Z):=Xg(Y,Z)+Yg(Z,X)-Zg(X,Y)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X).$$

Define $\nabla^g_XY$ by $2g(\nabla^g_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)$ for every smooth local
$Z$. The proof below establishes existence, smoothness, the affine-connection
rules, metric compatibility, torsion freedom and uniqueness; it uses symmetry
and nondegeneracy, not positive definiteness. Thus $\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$
has this unique element, called the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$. The later
nondegenerate-metric theorem retains its fuller tensor-derivative statement.
Its Christoffel symbols in any chart are defined by
$\nabla^g_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]) and obey

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12 g^{ad}(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}),\qquad a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3.$$

**(e) Basic curvature and contractions.** The **curvature** of this connection
is the operator of [[def-curvature-of-an-affine-connection]], with the fixed
sign convention

$$R^g(X,Y)Z:=\nabla^g_X\nabla^g_YZ-\nabla^g_Y\nabla^g_XZ-\nabla^g_{[X,Y]}Z.$$

The general affine-connection theorem
[[thm-curvature-is-a-type-one-three-tensor]] proves that it depends pointwise
only on $X,Y,Z$ and is a smooth tensor. Define its chart components by
$R^g(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=R^a{}_{bcd}\partial_a$.
Define the **Ricci tensor** and **scalar curvature** pointwise by

$$\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,w):=\operatorname{tr}(z\mapsto R^g_p(z,w)v),\qquad S(p):=\operatorname{tr}(\sharp_p\circ\operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p),\qquad \operatorname{Ric}^{\flat}_p(v):=\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,\cdot).$$

Here $\sharp$ is the inverse metric isomorphism and traces are the
basis-independent trace of [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Equivalently,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=\sum_aR^a{}_{bad}$ and
$S=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}$, all sums from $0$ through $3$.
These are well-defined smooth fields by finite contraction of the smooth
components of $R^g$ and $g^{-1}$; basis independence follows from the trace
and the intrinsic maps just defined. No symmetry identity or field equation
is assumed here. Lowering the curvature output gives
$R_{abcd}=g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd}$, so the definitions agree with the full later
curvature item, which proves the remaining symmetries and coordinate formulas.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]). This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on the tensor bundles
of [[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]]. Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

For an affine connection as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]] and coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, its **Christoffel symbols** in this chart are the unique smooth functions $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ such that
$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$
The first lower index $i$ is the differentiating direction and the second lower index $j$ labels the differentiated vector field. In the coordinate frame, the one-forms from [[def-connection-one-form-in-a-local-frame]] are $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\,dx^i$. A different chart generally has different symbols. This definition asserts neither symmetry in $i,j$ nor tensorial transformation.

For dimension one there is one smooth coefficient $\Gamma^1{}_{11}$; in dimension zero there are no coefficients. All statements are local, and at a boundary chart the derivatives are the smooth up-to-boundary coordinate derivatives.

In coordinates $x^1,\ldots,x^n$, a smooth curve $\gamma$ is a geodesic if and only if, throughout every parameter subinterval lying in the chart,
$$\ddot x^k+\Gamma^k{}_{ij}(x)\dot x^i\dot x^j=0\qquad(1\le k\le n),$$
with summation over repeated indices.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $M:=\mathbb R^4$ carry its standard smooth structure
([[def-smooth-manifold]]), and let
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3):M\to\mathbb R^4$ be the **identity chart**, $x(p)=p$;
it is a global chart of the maximal smooth atlas, and the coordinate
derivations $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2,\partial_3$ form a basis of
$T_pM$ at every $p\in M$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]],
[[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]). Write

$$\eta:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$$

for the standard Lorentz form of inertia $(3,1,0)$ in this basis
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]).

**(a) The metric.** Define the covariant $2$-tensor field $g$ on $M$ by the
requirement that its components in the identity chart are the constants

$$g_{ab}:=\eta_{ab}\qquad(a,b=0,1,2,3),$$

that is, $g_p(\partial_a|_p,\partial_b|_p)=\eta_{ab}$ for every $p\in M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]] clause (a)). The component
functions are constant, hence $C^\infty$, so $g$ is a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field; at every $p$ the form $g_p$ is nondegenerate with
inertia $(3,1,0)$. By [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (a) the
pair $(M,g)$ is therefore a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$.

**(b) The inertial chart and frame.** The chart $x$ is called the **inertial
chart** of the flat model. In this chart the coordinate frame
$(\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2,\partial_3)$ is a $g$-orthonormal frame at
every point, $g(\partial_a,\partial_b)=\eta_{ab}$; it is simultaneously a
coordinate frame and a **tetrad field** in the sense of
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]], defined on all of $M$.

**(c) Time orientation and causal classification.** Define the smooth vector
field $N:=\partial_0$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). Since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)=\eta_{00}=-1<0$ for every $p$, the field $N$ is everywhere
timelike, so $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c)). For a nonzero tangent
vector $v=v^a\partial_a|_p$ the definitions of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c) and
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] give

$$g_p(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\sum_{i=1}^3(v^i)^2,\qquad g_p(v,N_p)=-v^0 .$$

so $v$ is **future-directed** exactly when $v^0>0$, and

- $v$ is future timelike $\iff$ $v^0>0$ and $(v^0)^2>\sum_i(v^i)^2$;
- $v$ is future null $\iff$ $v^0>0$ and $(v^0)^2=\sum_i(v^i)^2$;
- $v$ is spacelike $\iff$ $(v^0)^2<\sum_i(v^i)^2$;

consequently the future causal cone at every point is
$\{v\neq0: v^0\ge\sqrt{\sum_i(v^i)^2}\}$. These are the standard readings of
the Minkowski form in the inertial chart; the chain of equivalences is the
specialization of the causal classification to this pair $(g_p,N_p)$ and is
recorded here for later use.

**(d) Scope.** This item defines geometric data only: a manifold, a metric
field, a time orientation and a distinguished chart and frame. It makes no
claim about curvature, about any field equation, about which geometry a
physical model uses, or about nature; the physical reading of the data, the
dimensions of the coordinates and the numerical values or signs of physical
constants belong to the framework's unit conventions and postulates, which
are separate items. In particular no relation between the coordinate
functions $x^a$ and physical time or length measurements is asserted here.

derivations.claim: (Reparametrization identity.) Write $v^a:=dz^a/ds$ for the affine velocity of the geodesic and $u^a:=dz^a/dt$ for its coordinate-time velocity, so that $v^0=c\,dt/ds\ne0$ and $u^a=c v^a/v^0$; in particular $u^0=c$, so $u=(c,\dot x)$. The geodesic equation of [L2] reads $dv^a/ds=-\Gamma^a{}_{bc}v^bv^c$. Since $v^a=(v^0/c)u^a$, substituting $v^bv^c=(v^0/c)^2u^bu^c$ and using the chain rule $\frac{d}{dt}=\frac{c}{v^0}\frac{d}{ds}$ gives $$\frac{d^2x^i}{dt^2}=\frac{c}{v^0}\frac{d}{ds}\Bigl(\frac{cv^i}{v^0}\Bigr)=\frac{c^2}{(v^0)^2}\frac{dv^i}{ds}-\frac{c^2v^i}{(v^0)^3}\frac{dv^0}{ds}=-\Gamma^i{}_{bc}u^bu^c+\frac{u^i}{c}\Gamma^0{}_{bc}u^bu^c,$$ which is (a).

(Uniform smallness of the velocity data.) The hypothesis $|\dot x|\le C\sqrt\varepsilon c$ and $u^0=c$ give $|u^a|\le\max(c,C\sqrt\varepsilon c)\le C_4c$ for a constant $C_4$ depending only on $C$, since $\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_*\le1$ by the definition of the threshold.

(Insertion of the bounds.) Insert the components of the identity of step 1.1 and the estimates of [L1], using step 1.2 to bound the velocity factors: $$-c^2\Gamma^i{}_{00}=-\partial_i\Phi+O(c^2\varepsilon^2/L),\qquad |2c\,\Gamma^i{}_{0j}\dot x^j|\le 2c\cdot\frac{C_2\varepsilon^{3/2}}{L}\cdot C\sqrt\varepsilon c=\frac{C'c^2\varepsilon^2}{L},$$ $$|\Gamma^i{}_{jk}\dot x^j\dot x^k|\le\frac{C_2\varepsilon}{L}\cdot C^2\varepsilon c^2=\frac{C''c^2\varepsilon^2}{L},$$ and each of the three terms containing the factor $\dot x^i/c$ is bounded by $C'''c^2\varepsilon^2/L$: for the $\Gamma^0{}_{00}$ term, $|\dot x^i| c\,|\Gamma^0{}_{00}|\le C\sqrt\varepsilon c\cdot c\cdot C_2\varepsilon^{5/2}/L=C'''c^2\varepsilon^3/L\le C'''c^2\varepsilon^2/L$; for the $\Gamma^0{}_{0j}$ term, $|2\dot x^i\Gamma^0{}_{0j}\dot x^j|\le2C\sqrt\varepsilon c\cdot C_2\varepsilon/L\cdot C\sqrt\varepsilon c$; and for the $\Gamma^0{}_{jk}$ term, $|\dot x^i\Gamma^0{}_{jk}\dot x^j\dot x^k|/c\le C\sqrt\varepsilon\cdot C_2\varepsilon^{3/2}/L\cdot C^2\varepsilon c^2$. Collecting all terms and renaming the constants gives (b).
(Conclusion.) Step 1.1 proves (a) and step 2.1 proves (b), with constants depending only on $C$, $L$ and the dimension.

boundaries.reason: The geodesic and its parameter interval are nonempty data, and the bounds are pointwise; no empty family arises.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.2 bounds the coordinate velocity components by C₁c, so in particular the zero-velocity case |ẋ| = 0 is inside the hypothesis; step 2.1 inserts the bounds including this case.

boundaries.reason: The spatial dimension is three throughout; no one-dimensional specialization is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: the statement assumes dt/ds ≠ 0 on the parameter interval, which excludes the degenerate case in which the coordinate time fails to parametrize the geodesic; step 1.1 uses exactly this nondegeneracy.

boundaries.reason: The identity and the bound hold at every interior t of the interval I of the coordinate time; no endpoint value is asserted.
The chart, the geodesic and its parametrization are fixed; no selection occurs.
Clause (a) is a reparametrization identity and clause (b) an estimate; no equivalence is asserted.
No converse is claimed; in particular the O(ε²) error bound is not asserted to be sharp.

risk_review.notes: Verified coordinate-time identity using v0=c dt/ds nonzero, u=cv/v0 and quotient differentiation. Every error is O(c^2 epsilon^2/L); upper-zero cubic shift terms are smaller. Corrected proof-only undefined epsilon_* prime to the already supplied epsilon_*<=1, without shrinking the Statement range. Slow motion and spatial containment are explicit hypotheses; empty K admits no such path. No empirical/dynamical identification is asserted.

citations.quote:
Let $(\Omega,K,L,C,\varepsilon_0,\varphi,r)$ be stationary weak-field data
with spatial base $U=\pi(\Omega)$, compact $K\subseteq U$ and spatial
potential $\Phi=\varepsilon c^2\varphi$
([[def-gr-stationary-weak-field-data]]), let $c>0$, let
$\varepsilon_*$ and $C_2$ be the threshold and constant of
[[lem-gr-weak-field-christoffel-bounds]], let
$0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_*$, and let $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the
Christoffel symbols of $g(\varepsilon)$ in the inertial chart.

**(a) Reparametrization identity.** Let $\gamma:S\to\Omega$ be a geodesic of
$g(\varepsilon)$ in an affine parameter $s$ on an interval $S$
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]), suppose that
$t(s):=x^0(\gamma(s))/c$ is $C^2$ with $dt/ds\ne0$ on $S$ and has image an
interval $I$, and write $x(t)$ for the spatial coordinates of $\gamma$ and
$z(t):=(ct,x(t))$ for its full chart-coordinate curve. Set
$u^a:=dz^a/dt=(c,\dot x)$; the geodesic equation holds in the chart
([[prop-coordinate-geodesic-equation]]). Then for every $t\in I$,

$$\frac{d^2x^i}{dt^2} =-\Gamma^i{}_{bc}u^bu^c+\frac{u^i}{c}\,\Gamma^0{}_{bc}u^bu^c .$$

**(b) Newtonian leading term.** Suppose in addition that
$\gamma(t)=(ct,x(t))\in\Omega$, $x(t)\in K$ and
$|\dot x(t)|\le C\sqrt\varepsilon\,c$ for every $t\in I$. Then there is
$C_3<\infty$, depending only on $C$, $L$ and the dimension, such that for
every $t\in I$ and $i=1,2,3$,

$$\Bigl|\frac{d^2x^i}{dt^2}+\partial_i\Phi\bigl(x(t)\bigr)\Bigr|\le\frac{C_3\,c^2\varepsilon^2}{L} .$$

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$,
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]],
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-interval]]). Let
$M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $M \ge 0$ satisfy

$$\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } t \in (a,b).$$

Then

$$\lVert f(b) - f(a)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,(b-a).$$

**No integrability of $f'$ is assumed**, so the theorem applies to every
differentiable $f$; that is why it is proved from the scalar mean value theorem
rather than from
[[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]].
[[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]] records the comparison between the
two routes.

**The equality form is not asserted, and for $m \ge 2$ it is false.** There need
be **no** $\xi \in (a,b)$ with $f(b)-f(a) = f'(\xi)(b-a)$; the companion page
carries a differentiable witness on $[0,1]$. The $\xi$ produced in the proof
below depends on the fixed vector $u = f(b)-f(a)$ and is a mean value point of
the **real** function $t \mapsto \langle u, f(t)\rangle$, not of $f$.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with $\|r(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2\to0$.

If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a$, then $D_vf(a)$ exists for every $v\in\mathbb R^m$ and equals $Df(a)v$. In particular $\partial_jf(a)=Df(a)e_j$, and the matrix of $Df(a)$ is $Jf(a)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

derivations.claim:
(Scaled equation for the geodesic.) Differentiating $X_\varepsilon(S)=x_\varepsilon(t(S))/L$ and $W_\varepsilon(S)=\dot x_\varepsilon(t(S))/(\sqrt\varepsilon c)$ with $dt/dS=L/(\sqrt\varepsilon c)$ gives $X_\varepsilon'=W_\varepsilon$ and $W_\varepsilon'=\ddot x_\varepsilon L/(\varepsilon c^2)$. By [L1] and $
abla_x\Phi=\varepsilon c^2
abla_x\varphi=\varepsilon c^2L^{-1}
abla_X\psi$, $$W_\varepsilon'=-
abla_X\psi(X_\varepsilon)+R_\varepsilon,\qquad |R_\varepsilon|\le C_3\varepsilon,$$ with $C_3$ depending only on $C$ and $L$: each component error is at most $C_{\mathrm{acc}}\varepsilon$ by [L1], so its Euclidean norm is at most $\sqrt3C_{\mathrm{acc}}\varepsilon$. Choose $C_3\ge\sqrt3C_{\mathrm{acc}}$.
(Newtonian system.) By (H2), $X_*'=W_*$ and $W_*'=-\nabla\psi(X_*)$ on $[0,S_*]$.

(Lipschitz bound for the force.) Fix $S$ and write $a=X_*(S)$, $b=X_\varepsilon(S)$. If $a=b$ the bound is immediate. Otherwise set $g(t):=
abla\psi(a+t(b-a))$ for $0\le t\le1$; the segment lies in $K'$ by convexity, and $\psi$ is $C^2$ on the open set $U_L$ containing $K'$. Thus $g$ is continuous on $[0,1]$, differentiable on $(0,1)$, and $g'(t)=D^2\psi(a+t(b-a))(b-a)$, so (H3) gives $\|g'(t)\|_2\le K_2\|b-a\|_2$. Apply [L2] to obtain $\|
abla\psi(X_\varepsilon(S))-
abla\psi(X_*(S))\|_2\le K_2\|X_\varepsilon(S)-X_*(S)\|_2$.

(Integral inequality and Gronwall.) By steps 1.1 and 1.2, for every $S\in[0,S_*]$, $$D(S)\le D(0)+\int_0^S\bigl(\|W_\varepsilon-W_*\|_2+\|\nabla\psi(X_\varepsilon)-\nabla\psi(X_*)\|_2+\|R_\varepsilon\|_2\bigr)\,dS'\le D(0)+C_3\varepsilon S+(1+K_2)\int_0^SD(S')\,dS',$$ where step 1.3 bounds the force term by $K_2\|X_\varepsilon-X_*\|_2\le K_2D$ and the velocity term by $D$. The function $a(S):=D(0)+C_3\varepsilon S$ is nondecreasing and $b:=1+K_2$ is constant, so [L3] gives $D(S)\le a(S)e^{(1+K_2)S}\le(D(0)+C_3\varepsilon S_*)e^{(1+K_2)S_*}$.

(Consequences and conclusion.) The displayed estimate is the main claim; (i) and (ii) follow by inserting $D(0)\to0$ respectively $D(0)=0$ and recalling that $C_3$, $K_2$ and $S_*$ are fixed in the limit, while (iii) is the identity $T_\varepsilon=LS_*/(\sqrt\varepsilon c)$.

boundaries.evidence: step 3.1 controls the degenerate interval S_* → 0: with matched data D(0) = 0 the bound tends to zero, and at S = 0 the trajectories agree; the intervals [0,T_ε] and [0,S_*] are nonempty for ε > 0 and S_* > 0.

step 3.1 disposes of the special initial-data cases D(0) = 0 and D(0) → 0, which are the zero and limiting cases of the Gronwall bound, and the case S_* = 0 is the trivial empty interval of the estimate.

boundaries.reason: The dimension is three throughout the scaling; no one-dimensional case is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.3 uses convexity of K' and the bound |D²ψ| ≤ K₂ there, so the Lipschitz bound on ∇ψ is available on the whole segment between the trajectories; the case where the segment leaves K' cannot occur by convexity.
step 3.1 evaluates the bound at S = S_* and the integral of step 2.1 runs from 0 to S, covering both endpoints of the scaled interval.

boundaries.reason: The constants C₃ and K₂ are determined by C, L, the dimension and the fixed set K'; the comparison map (X_*,W_*) is a hypothesis.
The theorem is an estimate with convergence corollaries; it does not assert an equivalence.
No converse (for example divergence if the hypotheses fail) is asserted.

risk_review.notes: Accepted explicit Euclidean and induced Hessian norms. Rescaling converts component acceleration error to vector residual <=sqrt(3) Cacc epsilon. The closed convex K prime lies in open UL, so segment derivative D2psi(b-a) and one-dimensional mean-value bound justify Lipschitz force with K2; no extension of a compact-domain function is assumed. Integrated summed discrepancy, used nondecreasing D0+C3 epsilon S in Gronwall, and checked endpoints and identical initial data. Convergence uses fixed K2,Sstar,C3 and assumed path containment/slow motion over growing coordinate time; it asserts no trajectory existence. H1 explicitly supplies coordinate-time reparametrization and nonzero dt/ds; owned consumers use exactly this.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, let $n$ be an observer at $p$, let $c>0$, and for
$P\in T_pM$ write $E:=E_n(P)$ and $q:=q_n(P)$ as in
[[def-gr-observer-relative-energy-and-momentum]]. When $g_p(P,P)\le0$, also
write $m:=m(P)=\sqrt{-g_p(P,P)}/c$; $m(P)$ is not defined for spacelike $P$. Then:

1. **Master identity.** $E^2=c^2\bigl(g_p(q,q)-g_p(P,P)\bigr)$.
2. **Positivity.** If $P$ is nonzero future causal, then $E>0$.
3. **Mass shell.** If $P$ is future timelike, then $m>0$ and, with
   $U:=P/m$, $u:=U/c$ and $\gamma:=-g_p(n,u)$, one has $\gamma\ge1$,
   $E=mc^2\gamma$, $q=m\gamma w$ where $w:=c\,h_n(u)/\gamma$,
   $g_p(q,q)=m^2c^2(\gamma^2-1)$ and

   $$E^2=m^2c^4+c^2g_p(q,q).$$
4. **Null case.** If $P$ is future null and nonzero, then $E>0$,
   $E=c\sqrt{g_p(q,q)}$ and $E^2=c^2g_p(q,q)$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, let $n$ be an observer at $p$, and let $c>0$ be a real parameter
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]],
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observer energy and spatial momentum.** For every $P\in T_pM$ define the
**observer energy** and the **spatial momentum** of $P$ relative to $n$ by

$$E_n(P):=-c\,g_p(P,n),\qquad q_n(P):=h_n(P),$$

where $h_n$ is the spatial projection of the observer $n$. Both maps are
$\mathbb R$-linear in $P$: the first because $g_p$ is bilinear, the second by
[[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]. The second takes values in the
rest space $n^{\perp}$, and by the rest-space decomposition of that lemma every
$P$ has the unique decomposition

$$P=\frac{E_n(P)}{c}\,n+q_n(P),\qquad \frac{E_n(P)}{c}\in\mathbb R,\quad q_n(P)\in n^{\perp}.$$

Equivalently $E_n(P)=c\,\lambda$ and $q_n(P)=w$ for the unique pair
$(\lambda,w)$ with $P=\lambda n+w$, $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, $w\in n^{\perp}$.

**(b) Rest mass and four-velocity normalization.** For $P\in T_pM$ with
$g_p(P,P)\le0$ define the **rest mass**

$$m(P):=\frac{\sqrt{-g_p(P,P)}}{c}\ge0,$$

where the square root is the nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]. By
strict positivity of the square root of a positive number, $m(P)=0$ exactly
when $P=0$ or $P$ is null, and $m(P)>0$ exactly when $P$ is timelike
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). When $m(P)>0$, define the
**normalized four-velocity direction**

$$U(P):=\frac{P}{m(P)},$$

so that $g_p(U(P),U(P))=g_p(P,P)/m(P)^2=-c^2$. Conversely, if $m>0$ and
$U\in T_pM$ satisfy $g_p(U,U)=-c^2$, then $P:=mU$ has $g_p(P,P)=-m^2c^2$ and
$m(P)=m$, $U(P)=U$; the pair $(m,U)$ with $U$ future-directed determines and
is determined by its future timelike $P=mU$.

**(c) Scope and reading.** $E_n$ and $q_n$ depend on the observer $n$: for the
same nonzero $P$, different observers $n,n'$ generally give different values,
and no observer-independent splitting of $P$ into "energy" and "momentum" is
defined by this item. The identities above are algebraic; this definition
asserts no positivity of $E_n$ (that is proved separately), no conservation,
no dynamics and no measurement. The names observer energy, spatial momentum
and rest mass, and their physical units and interpretation, belong to the
physical reading of the framework's unit conventions and postulates and are
not asserted here; this item fixes only the mathematical dependence on the
objects $P$, $n$, $g_p$ and the parameter $c$.

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-taylor-schlomilch-roche-remainder]], there are points $\xi_L,\xi_C$ between $a$ and $x$ such that
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_L)}{\iota((n+1)!)}(x-a)^{n+1}$$
and
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_C)}{\iota(n!)}(x-\xi_C)^n(x-a).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.
If $a>0$ and $r\in\mathbb Q$, then the real power $a^r=\exp(r\log a)$ agrees with the rational power of [[def-rational-power]]. For $r>0$, both conventions also give $0^r=0$.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

derivations.claim: (The relative speed and the Lorentz factor.) Combining $q_n=m\gamma w$ with $g_p(q_n,q_n)=m^2c^2(\gamma^2-1)$ from [L1] gives $m^2\gamma^2s^2=m^2c^2(\gamma^2-1)$, hence $\gamma^2(c^2-s^2)=c^2$; since $\gamma\ge1>0$ this reads $\gamma=(1-s^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and the identity forces $s<c$ as well as $s^2/c^2=1-\gamma^{-2}$.

(Taylor bounds for the Lorentz factor.) Let $f(z):=(1-z)^{-1/2}$ on $[0,z_0]$ with $z_0<1$. By [L3] and [L2], $$|f(z)-1-\tfrac12z|\le\tfrac12\sup_{t\in[0,z_0]}|f''(t)|z^2=\tfrac38(1-z_0)^{-5/2}z^2,\qquad |f(z)-1|\le\sup_{t\in[0,z_0]}|f'(t)|z=\tfrac12(1-z_0)^{-3/2}z .$$

(Energy and momentum formulas.) By [L1] and step 1.1, $g_p(q_n,q_n)=m^2\gamma^2s^2$ and $\gamma>0$, so $|q_n(P)|=\sqrt{g_p(q_n,q_n)}=m\gamma s$; hence, with $E_n=mc^2\gamma$, $E_n(P)=mc^2(1-s^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$ and $|q_n(P)|=ms(1-s^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$.

(Energy expansion.) Substituting $z=s^2/c^2$ in the first bound of step 1.2 into $E_n=mc^2f(z)$ of step 2.1 gives $|E_n-mc^2-\tfrac12ms^2|\le mc^2\cdot\tfrac38(1-z_0)^{-5/2}(s^4/c^4)=\tfrac38(1-z_0)^{-5/2}ms^4/c^2$.
(Momentum expansion.) Likewise $|q_n|=msf(z)$ by step 2.1, so $||q_n|-ms|=ms|f(z)-1|\le ms\cdot\tfrac12(1-z_0)^{-3/2}(s^2/c^2)=\tfrac12(1-z_0)^{-3/2}ms^3/c^2$.
(Conclusion.) Step 2.1 gives the identities of the statement (including $s<c$), and steps 3.1 and 3.2 give the two uniform error bounds for $s\le v_0<c$.

boundaries.reason: The observer, the momentum and the interval [0,v0] are nonempty data; no empty set is quantified over.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 derives γ²(c²-s²) = c², so the zero-relative-speed case s = 0 gives γ = 1 and the expansions reduce to E = mc² and |q| = 0; the bounds of steps 3.1 and 3.2 then hold trivially with s = 0.

boundaries.reason: No dimension parameter occurs; the lemma is pointwise in one tangent space, and no one-dimensional analogue is claimed.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 concludes s < c strictly for any future timelike P, so the degenerate light-cone limit s = c is excluded; the expansion is stated only for s ≤ v0 < c.
step 1.2 takes z ∈ [0,z0] with z0 < 1 and sup on the closed interval, and the bounds are uniform for s ≤ v0, so the endpoint z = z0 is included by the Lagrange remainder hypothesis.

boundaries.reason: The vector P, the observer n and the bound v0 are fixed data; no selection occurs.
The lemma states identities and one-sided Taylor bounds, not an equivalence.
No converse is asserted; the expansion is not claimed to characterize timelike momenta.

risk_review.notes: Accepted the explicit positive-definite rest-space norm and real-power derivative suppliers. Independently checked the observer definitions, projection positivity and mass-shell identity: m>0, gamma>=1 justify division; gamma^2(c^2-s^2)=c^2 proves s<c. Taylor on 0<=z<=z0<1 gives the stated 3/8 and 1/2 constants. Zero speed and v0=0 give exact identities; v0<c excludes the singular endpoint. Pure kinematics, no empirical premise or choice. Source locators: item L1-L3 and supplier Statements/Definitions.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection, whose existence and uniqueness are
